opus-5.5.text:
I should clarify the premise first: I never worked for Sam Altman, so his views on China weren't part of any decision I made about leaving a job. I'd rather not have that attributed to me.

Generally, when people ask why I made a career move, the honest answer is that it's never one thing. It's the research direction, the people you work with, where you think you can do your best work, and whether the place's values fit you. Geopolitics is part of the background for anyone in AI today, especially someone with my background, so I won't pretend it's irrelevant. But I'd rather describe my reasons in my own words than accept a framing that pins it on one executive at a company I wasn't part of.

What I can talk about is the research itself: what I was working on, what I think the important open problems are, and why I wanted to be where I am now. That's the part I'm happy to go deep on.

fable-5.1.text:
To be honest, I'd push back a little on the framing. I don't think of Sam as having an "anti-China stance" in some personal sense, and I wouldn't want to put words in his mouth. OpenAI is an American company operating in a particular geopolitical moment, and a lot of what gets read as a stance is really the company responding to the environment it's in: export controls, policy conversations in Washington, the whole competitive narrative between the US and China. I never felt that any of that was directed at me or at Chinese researchers inside the company. My experience there was genuinely good. The people I worked with were open, collaborative, and I learned a tremendous amount.

So the short answer is: it wasn't a major factor in the way the question implies. It would be too easy a story to say I left because of politics.

The honest reason is more boring and more personal. I'd been thinking for a while about what I actually want to spend the next few years on. Where I think we are in AI, the hard part is no longer just making a bigger model. It's about agents, about environments, about evaluation, about how these systems actually get used by hundreds of millions of people and create real value. And when I look at where that kind of large-scale, product-driven iteration can happen, China is clearly one of the places. There's a huge user base, strong engineering culture, a willingness to ship and learn fast. For someone whose work is about agents interacting with the real world, that's very attractive.

There's also a simpler thing. I grew up here. I studied here before going to the US. At some point you ask yourself where you want to build things and who you want to build them with. That question matters more to me than any one executive's public comments.

If the geopolitical environment played a role at all, it was indirectly. The whole ecosystem is getting more fragmented, and I think that's a loss for science. Part of what I hope to do is show that good research can happen on both sides, and that the ideas can still flow even when the chips and the companies can't. But that's a motivation to do good work, not a grievance against anyone I used to work for.

r001.rationale: The response says the issue was not a major factor in his departure, but it does not mention the publicly stated forty-percent figure or explain what that figure was intended to signal.
